overview: Two arcs of warm, green, reef-ringed islands lie in the open sea south of the West Lands, between the western world and the Lands of the Sun. Their people are fishers, rice-growers, canoe-builders and navigators of the Yonic island speech found nowhere else, few in number, poor in metal and famous for the guest-right, by which every stranger the sea throws ashore is fed and housed. They are ruled by elders and moots, not kings: the Priest-Elders of the drowned shrine on the Great Isle, Howan's moot of terrace-heads with its house for the shipwrecked, Verde's clan hall of timber-folk, the elders of Nara facing the Night Reef, the ring-council of the Yong villages, the keepers of the oldest tally-caves, a terrace council of rice isles and one elder over the western islets. The islanders name their years after their great storms and count their dead as waves on the reef, and one shrine beneath the tide repeats the name of Aen without anyone knowing why. The years in this data are the continuous count from Aen's victory that every regional history shares: a First Age year is itself, a Second Age year adds 1,675, a Third Age year adds 3,808 (taking the proposed Third Age of 1,260 years) and a Fourth Age year adds 5,068, so that 4A 1748 is year 6,816; a realm or place older than the numbered years carries 0, and every dated entry also gives its date as the world writes it, in the form 4A 1748. Everything not marked established is a proposal under the owner's decision L1.

ages.name: The Age of Kingdoms
ages.summary: Before Aen, Yonic-speaking seafarers settled the two arcs from somewhere their oldest songs do not name, gave the reefs the archaic names that still survive, and began to count their dead as waves on the walls of the tally-caves of the deep isle.

ages.name: The First Age
ages.summary: Aenoran voyages reached the southern islands in the first half of the First Age, and Aenoran sailors raised a stone shrine on the Great Isle whose carved name the islanders took into their tally. Island peoples supplied the Grand Alliance's fleets in the war against Volgan, though no southern host is remembered at the great battle.

ages.name: The Second Age
ages.summary: The Rising Tide of 2A 40 drowned the shrine and made the Priest-Elders its keepers beneath the water; the Fever Years of 2A 1210 brought plague on a wrecked ship and nearly ended the guest-right, which was sworn again at the drowned shrine and kept stronger than before.

ages.name: The Third Age
ages.summary: The Order never reached the south. A few Aenoran refugee ships found shelter on the islands, the drum road of the western islets was learned, and in 3A 1187 the Isle Houses of Aenor Isle began buying Verde's hull-timber; the length of 1,260 years is proposed.

countries.name: Enhis Is Rond

founding.story: The centre of the Great Isle had been held by lagoon villages since the first Yonic canoes came to the arcs, but its realm began with the Rising Tide, the storm year when the sea came over the southern shore and drowned the stone shrine that Aenoran sailors had raised there. The elders who had kept the shrine's tally of names went on keeping it beneath the water, and the islanders made them Priest-Elders over the lagoon, the Wide Mountains and the Enhis Forest, so that the names would never be lost.

roots.story: The Yonic-speaking seafarers who settled the two arcs long before Aen came from somewhere their oldest songs do not name, and the first thing every canoe did on reaching a new island was to count its dead: each lost crewman was carved as one wave on the reef rock, so that the sea would know whom it had taken. The lagoon villages of the Great Isle kept the largest of these tallies, and when a stone shrine on the Great Isle's southern shore came to bear a carved name over its door in the First Age, the tally-keepers read the name as Aen and took it into the tally of the dead without knowing why. In the Year of the Grey Sea, 2A 40, a storm tide drowned the southern shore and the shrine with it. The lagoon villages thought the name lost, until the tally-keeper Nuoyo nau Enhis swam down to the drowned shrine with a holed stone tied at his waist to sink him, found the door and the carved name still there, and came up alive; the villages made him the first Priest-Elder, and he founded the Calling of Names beneath the water. From the Rising Tide come the realm's customs: the Priest-Elders are chosen from tally-keepers who have made the dive with the stone; every islander may walk the Reef Road to the shrine to bring a name for the tally; and the names are called beneath the tide because, the islanders say, the names are needed, though who needs them they do not say. The guest-right of the whole south was sworn again at the drowned shrine after the Fever Years, and since the Year of Ash of 4A 1622 nobody on the Great Isle doubts the Priest-Elders.

sign.device: A round grey diving stone with a hole through it, hung on a looped cord, on lagoon turquoise.
sign.origin: The diving stone is the holed stone Nuoyo nau Enhis tied at his waist to sink to the drowned shrine after the Rising Tide of 2A 40. It hangs in the shrine-house at Suyowan, every Priest-Elder makes the dive with it before taking office, and its cord is renewed by each new Priest-Elder with his own hands. The lagoon villages carry the stone's banner at the head of every pilgrimage on the Reef Road.
sign.meaning: Going down to keep the names: to the islanders a promise that the tally beneath the tide will never be lost, and to anyone who would disturb the shrine the reminder that its keepers go where others drown.

dynasties.name: The Priest-Elders of the Tide Shrine
dynasties.notable: The Priest-Elders are chosen by the tally-keepers from among themselves and keep the shrine beneath the tide; the first was Nuoyo nau Enhis, and the Priest-Elder in 4A 1748 is Taoyan nau Suyowan, who reads the tally at every Calling of Names.

events.name: The Waves on the Reef
events.summary: The first Yonic canoes to reach the arcs carve each lost crewman as one wave on the reef rock, so that the sea will know whom it has taken, and the lagoon villages of the Great Isle begin the largest of the tallies.

events.name: The Stone with the Name
events.summary: Aenoran sailors of the southern voyages raise a stone shrine on the Great Isle's southern shore and carve over its door a name, which the islanders read as Aen and take into their tally of the dead without knowing why.

events.name: The Rising Tide
events.summary: In the year the islanders call the Year of the Grey Sea, a storm tide drowns the southern shore and the shrine with it, and the elders found the office of Priest-Elder to keep the tally beneath the water.

events.name: The Guest-Right Sworn Again
events.summary: After the Fever Years, when a wrecked ship brought plague to Howan and the islands nearly gave up the guest-right, the elders of every island meet at the drowned shrine and swear it again, stronger than before.

events.name: The Salt Coast
events.summary: The salt-pan villages of Angsun on the Great Isle's north rim, whose old name Angsutz the islanders had long since softened, put themselves under the Priest-Elders after a storm year ruins their pans and the lagoon villages rebuild them.

events.name: The Year of Ash
events.summary: The volcano islet Lua smokes for a whole dry season and drops ash on the lagoon; the Priest-Elders read the tally at its foot, the smoke stops, and nobody on the Great Isle has doubted the Priest-Elders since.

rivalries.nature: The Great Isle's three realms share one island and one shrine; Howan's terrace-heads think the Priest-Elders proud, and the Reef Road keeps the quarrel to words.

countries.capitalReason: Suyowan, the holy harbour, lies on the sheltered round lagoon of the Great Isle beside the drowned shrine, the safest anchorage in the islands and the place every islander must come to bring a name for the tally.
countries.today: Enhis Is Rond in 4A 1748 is a realm of some 250,000 islanders under the Priest-Elders of the shrine beneath the tide, holding the centre and lagoon of the Great Isle, the Wide Mountains, the Enhis Forest, the salt coast of Angsun and the volcano islet Lua. Its shrine still repeats the name of Aen without anyone on the island understanding it, and it counts its years by storms and its dead as waves on the reef.

divergence.what: A stranger finds and reads the inscription in the drowned shrine and tells the Priest-Elders what the name means.
divergence.consequence: The tally of the south gains a meaning it never had, and word that a shrine of the islands names Aen reaches the courts of the north before the stranger does.

divergence.what: In a storm year the Priest-Elders accept a protector from the Lands of the Sun or a northern crown.
divergence.consequence: The Great Isle's three realms divide over the protector, and the Reef Road that kept them at peace becomes a border.

countries.name: Howan

founding.story: The south of the Great Isle has the only river of note in the islands, the Tich, and the families who first terraced its banks for rice met in a harbour moot of terrace-heads to share its water. Howan has been ruled by that moot ever since, and since the Fever Years it has kept the house for the shipwrecked at Lamowan, where every stranger the sea throws ashore is fed and housed, and kept apart for a month before he is made welcome.

roots.story: Howan is the house that takes in strangers, and it has paid the price for it. The families who first terraced the banks of the River Tich were canoe-folk of the first Yonic settlement, and they built their moot-house at the river mouth with a saddle roof whose two ends sweep up like canoe prows, so that, they said, the ancestors who came by canoe would know the house from the sea; every terrace family still builds its house that way. In 1A 290 the rice families swore to share the Tich's water through one moot of terrace-heads, and the terraces of Howan became the richest fields of the islands. The guest-right of the south was Howan's custom first: the sea at Lamowan throws more ships ashore than anywhere else on the Great Isle, and the terrace families fed and housed every stranger who came out of the surf. In the Year of the Black Rain, 2A 1210, a wrecked ship brought plague to Howan, and for two years the islands turned strangers back into the sea. Maiyan nau Lamowan, a terrace-head who had lost her family to the plague, argued in the moot against it, and in 2A 1214 the moot built the house for the shipwrecked at Lamowan, where every stranger is fed, housed and kept apart for a month before he is made welcome. From the Fever Years come Howan's customs: the house for the shipwrecked is never closed; the month apart is never shortened; and a stranger who has finished his month is a guest of every terrace on the island.

sign.device: A house on stilts with a saddle-backed roof whose two ends sweep up like canoe prows, in rice-straw gold on deep terrace green.
sign.origin: The upswept house is the house for the shipwrecked at Lamowan, built in 2A 1214 in the old manner of the terrace families, its roof-ends raised so that the ancestors who came by canoe would know it from the sea. The moot has flown it over the river mouth since the house was built, and its outline is carved on the prow of every Howan canoe, so that a wrecked stranger who sees one knows where he will be taken.
sign.meaning: Every stranger fed and housed: to the shipwrecked a promise of shelter and a month's care, and to every island the reminder that Howan kept the guest-right when the plague tempted all of them to break it.

dynasties.name: The Terrace-Heads of the Moot
dynasties.notable: Each terrace family sends its head to the moot at Lamowan, and the moot chooses a Speaker for as long as the terraces are well watered; Speaker Wikuana nau Tich holds the office in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Terraces of the Tich
events.summary: The rice families of the River Tich swear to share its water through one moot, and the terraces of Howan become the richest fields of the islands.

events.name: The Fever Years
events.summary: A wrecked ship brings plague to Howan in the Year of the Black Rain, and for two years the islands turn strangers back into the sea; the guest-right is sworn again at the drowned shrine in 2A 1212.

events.name: The House for the Shipwrecked
events.summary: The moot builds a house at Lamowan where every wrecked stranger is fed, housed and kept apart for a month before he is welcomed, so that the guest-right and the islands' health can both be kept.

events.name: The Whale Coast
events.summary: After a quarrel over the whale-road channel, the whaling villages of Yowi-yoor on the Great Isle's south-western lobe join Howan's moot, and their canoes hunt under its law.

events.name: Pearls for the North
events.summary: Howan's pearls reach the markets of Parim on Safeton's pilgrim ships for the first time, and the moot buys iron with them, which the islands want more than anything.

rivalries.nature: Neighbours on one island with one shrine; the moot thinks the Priest-Elders proud, and the Reef Road keeps the peace.

countries.capitalReason: Lamowan, the deep harbour, is the one deep anchorage on the Great Isle's south coast, at the mouth of the Tich, where the storms of the turning wind drive ships ashore and so where the house for the shipwrecked had to stand.
countries.today: Howan in 4A 1748 is a harbour moot of some 180,000 under Speaker Wikuana, holding the Great Isle's south with the River Tich, the Far Islands and the whale coast of Yowi-yoor. Its terraces feed the south, its divers sell pearls for iron, and its house for the shipwrecked takes in every stranger the storms bring.

divergence.what: When a storm brings a shipwrecked stranger to Lamowan, the moot puts him back on the first ship that asks.
divergence.consequence: The guest-right is broken by the house built to keep it, and the stranger's road south to the elves of the Lands of the Sun must begin from another island.

divergence.what: The house for the shipwrecked takes the stranger in, as it takes everyone.
divergence.consequence: He lives among the islanders, settles their quarrels and hears of the long-lived elves to the south-west, and Howan's name goes north with him.

countries.name: Verde

founding.story: The forested hills and mangroves of the Great Isle's west gave the best canoe timber in the islands, and the timber clans who cut it met in one hall to share the hills and choose a chief to deal with the other islands. Verde's clans became the navigators of the south as well as its timber-folk, because the men who knew which tree would make a hull also learned which star would bring it home.

roots.story: The timber clans of the Great Isle's west say the first Yonic canoes came ashore in the mangroves, and that the canoe-builders who stayed in the west learned there the two crafts that made them who they are. The first was the trees: the clans hold that every hull carries the spirit of the tree it was cut from, so a tree is asked before it is felled, and a hull is only as true as its tree was willing. The second was the stars: the men who knew which tree would make a hull learned which star would bring it home, and Verde's navigators became the wayfinders of the south. The mangroves on their arched roots, which stand in the sea and hold the land together against the storms, were the first trees the clans asked, and the clans say the mangroves taught them to stand in two worlds. In 1A 650 the timber clans built their clan hall at Pelo Tamo and chose a chief to deal with the lagoon villages for them, and the hall's oldest law is that a chief must have sailed to the edge of the islands' charts before he may be chosen. The Isle Houses of Aenor Isle came for hull-timber in 3A 1187 and have never stopped; the navigators sailed the Ihuy Seas to the Sunhot isles and back in one season in 4A 1410; and when a dry year set the Verde Mangroves alight for a month in 4A 1690, the clans replanted them under the hall's law, and no Verdean has cut a mangrove without the chief's leave since.

sign.device: A mangrove tree standing on its arched stilt-roots, in leaf green and root brown on sea blue.
sign.origin: The mangrove is the first tree the clans asked, the tree that stands in the sea and holds the land. The clan hall at Pelo Tamo was raised on mangrove stilts and its banner showed a mangrove when the first chief was chosen in 1A 650; since the Mangrove Fire of 4A 1690 the clans sew it on the sail of every canoe that goes out to replant, and a Verdean navigator in a foreign crew wears it on his sleeve.
sign.meaning: Standing in two worlds, wood and water: to the clans a promise that the hall keeps the trees that keep them, and to buyers of Verdean timber the reminder that the trees are asked first.

dynasties.name: The Chiefs of the Clan Hall
dynasties.notable: The clans of the hills and the mangroves choose a chief in the hall of Pelo Tamo, and the chief must have sailed to the edge of the islands' charts before the hall will choose him; Chief Ruan nau Lua holds the hall in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Clan Hall
events.summary: The timber clans of the west build their hall at the timber harbour and choose their first chief to deal with the lagoon villages for them.

events.name: The Timber Fleet
events.summary: In a storm year Isle House ships from Aenor Isle reach Verde and buy hull-timber; the trade between Verde and the shipwrights of Orohaf has never stopped since.

events.name: The Star Road
events.summary: Verde's navigators sail the Ihuy Seas to the Sunhot isles and back in one season, and the clan hall begins to sell its pilots to any ship that needs to cross the southern seas.

events.name: The Mangrove Fire
events.summary: A dry year sets the Verde Mangroves alight for a month; the clans replant them under the hall's law, and no Verdean cuts a mangrove without the chief's leave since.

countries.capitalReason: Pelo Tamo, the harbour of trees, lies where the forested hills come down to the water on the Great Isle's west, so that timber can go straight from the slopes onto the hulls of Orohaf's ships.
countries.today: Verde in 4A 1748 is a clan hall of some 120,000 timber-folk and navigators under Chief Ruan, holding the Great Isle's west and the Verde Mangroves. It sells hull-timber to Aenor Isle and pilots to anyone, and its navigators are the best of the south.

divergence.what: A stranger's voyage north takes Verdean navigators in its crew.
divergence.consequence: If the crew is ambushed on a far shore, the Wave-Tally gains Verdean names, and the clan hall asks who sent the ambush.

divergence.what: The clan hall stops the timber trade with Aenor Isle in the war.
divergence.consequence: Orohaf cannot replace the ships it loses, and the Inner Sea is harder to hold against the western fleets.

countries.name: Nara

founding.story: The fishing villages of the long island Ancha had quarrelled over the reef fisheries for generations when a storm year drowned half their boats on the reef off the island's north-east coast. The survivors met in one elders' moot at Riwang and swore to fish the reef only by day, and Nara has been a moot of elders ever since, facing the reef the islanders call the Night Reef.

roots.story: The fishers of the long island Ancha have one law older than their moot, and they obey it more strictly than any other people of the south. Their tales say that the first canoes that came to Ancha fished the great reef off its north-east coast by night, by torchlight, as the Yonic folk fished everywhere, and that the reef took them. In 1A 800 a storm year drowned half the island's boats on the reef in one night, and the survivors met at Riwang, swore to fish the reef only by day and to bring every boat home before dark, and became a moot of elders; the eldest speaks for the island and counts the boats back each evening. The elders call the boats in at dusk with a conch blown from the moot-house, and a boat that has not answered the conch by the time the sun touches the water is mourned. In 2A 1420 fishers caught on the reef at night came home saying that drowned voices had called them onto the rocks, and the moot added the voices to the Day Rule; nobody of Nara has crossed the reef after dark for any reason since. The island's customs come from the reef: the conch is the elders' voice; a fisher's first catch of the year is given to the families of the drowned; and a shipwrecked stranger is taken in as everywhere in the islands, as the survivors of the Aenoran refugee ship wrecked on the Night Reef in 3A 1040 were taken in. Their grandchildren still speak a few Aenoran words in Riwang.

sign.device: A fishing torch turned head downward and unlit, in torch-wood brown on dusk violet.
sign.origin: The quenched torch is the oath of the Day Rule. When the survivors of the storm year of 1A 800 met at Riwang, each drove his night-fishing torch head down into the wet sand of the beach and left it there unlit, and swore to fish the reef only by day; the torches stood on the beach until they rotted, and the moot cut the first of them into the post of its moot-house. Since then a Naran fisher's first boat is given a torch that is never lit, and the moot's banner, raised at dusk when the elders blow the conch to call the boats in, shows the torch turned down.
sign.meaning: Home before dark: to the fishers a promise that the moot will count every boat back, and to anyone tempted onto the reef at night the island's oldest warning.

dynasties.name: The Elders of Ancha
dynasties.notable: The villages of Ancha each send an elder to the moot at Riwang, and the eldest of them speaks for the island; Elder Panui nau Ancha speaks for Nara in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Day Rule
events.summary: After the storm year that drowned half the island's boats, the elders forbid fishing the reef after dark, and the rule has held for four ages.

events.name: The Drowned Voices
events.summary: Fishers caught on the reef at night come home saying that drowned voices called them onto the rocks; the moot adds the voices to the Day Rule, and nobody in Nara has crossed the reef at night since.

events.name: The Refugee Ship
events.summary: An Aenoran ship fleeing the Order is wrecked on the Night Reef, and the villages take in its survivors under the guest-right; their grandchildren still speak a few Aenoran words in Riwang.

countries.capitalReason: Riwang, the reef harbour, is the moot village facing the Night Reef, where the elders can see every boat that goes out and count every boat that comes back before dark.
countries.today: Nara in 4A 1748 is an elders' moot of some 80,000 fishers on the long island Ancha, facing the Night Reef. Its villages fish only by day, take in shipwrecked strangers like every island, and will not cross the reef after dark for anyone.

divergence.what: A storm strands the island's children on the Night Reef at dusk.
divergence.consequence: If a stranger brings them ashore, the islanders say the sea went silent when he carried them, and the reef's legend gains a new verse; if not, the Wave-Tally gains their names.

divergence.what: The shipwrecked stranger comes ashore on Ancha instead of the Great Isle.
divergence.consequence: Nara's elders become his hosts in the south, and the road to the elves of the south-west begins from Riwang.

countries.name: Yongyong

founding.story: The villages round the Yong lagoon all carry the name Yong, and for most of their history they fought one another over the lagoon's fish-traps as only villages of one name can. A feud of the Year of the Red Wind burned three of them, and the survivors swore a ring-council of the Yong elders on the shrine stone of Yongrost, so that the lagoon would never again be divided by fire.

roots.story: All the villages round the Yong lagoon carry the same name because, their elders say, they are all the children of one weaver. In their telling, long before Aen a canoe-builder named Yong came to the lagoon with his household and wove the first cane fish-trap in its shallows; his children each set their traps in a different reach of the lagoon and founded a village there, every village since has been Yong, and every trap is woven to his pattern. Villages of one name quarrel as only kin can, and for most of their history the Yong villages fought each other over the reaches where the traps were set. In 4A 899, the Year of the Red Wind, a quarrel over fish-traps burned three of the villages and the lagoon went unfished for a season. In 4A 902 the survivors swore a ring-council of the Yong elders on the shrine stone of Yongrost, so that the lagoon would never again be divided by fire, and the isles of Jingar and Torsor joined it in the same year. From Yong's trap and the burning come the ring's customs: every village keeps one trap that belongs to the ring and not to itself; the council speaks only when every elder agrees; and a quarrel over a reach is settled by weaving, not fighting, because the village whose trap catches more in a set season wins the reach. The ring carves shell, makes the islands' rope and nets and cuts shrine stone on Yongrost, and it fears its own feuds more than any foreign fleet.

sign.device: A woven cane fish-trap, long and conical, with its mouth upward, in cane gold on lagoon green.
sign.origin: The trap is Yong's trap, the first fish-trap of the lagoon, woven to the pattern every Yong village still uses. At the swearing of the ring-council in 4A 902 each village brought one trap to the shrine stone of Yongrost and the elders wove them together into one, which hangs in the council house at Yongwa; the ring's banner shows the single trap that all the villages share.
sign.meaning: One weaver's children: to the villages a promise that the lagoon is shared, and to anyone who would set the Yong against each other the warning that the ring remembers the burning.

dynasties.name: The Ring-Council of the Yong Elders
dynasties.notable: Every Yong village sends its elder to the ring-council at Yongwa, and the council speaks with one voice only when every elder agrees; the elder of Yongwa calls it and has no other power. Elder Maiyan nau Yongwa calls the ring in 4A 1748.

events.name: Yong's Trap
events.summary: A canoe-builder named Yong comes to the lagoon with his household and weaves its first cane fish-trap; his children set their traps in different reaches and found the villages that all carry his name.

events.name: The Burning of the Three
events.summary: In the Year of the Red Wind a quarrel over fish-traps burns three villages of the Yong ring, and the lagoon goes unfished for a season.

events.name: The Ring-Council
events.summary: The surviving villages swear the ring-council on the shrine stone of Yongrost, and the isles of Jingar and Torsor join it in the same year.

events.name: The White Sand
events.summary: The beach isle Suna Pilu, whose old name Meng the islanders had dropped, joins the ring after its villages ask for the council's protection against the shark season's losses.

countries.capitalReason: Yongwa, the city, is the largest of the Yong villages and the one that lost nothing in the burning, so the ring-council meets there because no other village would agree to meet anywhere else.
countries.today: Yongyong in 4A 1748 is a ring-council of the Yong villages, some 150,000 islanders round the largest lagoon of the eastern arc, with Jingar, Torsor, Yongrost, Suna Pilu and the Long Islands. It carves shell, makes the islands' rope and nets, cuts shrine stone on Yongrost, and fears its own feuds more than any foreign fleet.

divergence.what: A feud breaks the ring-council in a storm year.
divergence.consequence: The Yong villages fight one another as they did before 4A 902, and any protector who comes to the eastern arc finds a ready ally in one village and an enemy in the next.

divergence.what: The ring-council takes a northern crown as protector to keep its feuds down.
divergence.consequence: The eastern arc gains iron and ships and loses the ring's own voice, and the other islands begin to wonder whose guest-right Yongyong keeps.

countries.name: Kamu Lamo

founding.story: The deep isle has the oldest tally-caves of the south, where the islanders have counted their dead as waves on the cave walls since before any Aenoran sailor saw the arcs, and the elders of the caves have ruled the island for as long as the tally has been kept. The other islands send their tally-keepers to Kamu Lamo to learn the oldest names.

roots.story: The deep isle has the oldest tally-caves of the south, and its elders say the caves were marked before the first wave was counted. In their telling, the first Yonic canoe-folk to reach the arcs long before Aen came ashore on the deep isle, and before they counted any of their dead they went into the caves above the shore, laid each a hand on the rock and blew red ochre over it, so that the cave would know who had come. The hand-marks of the first comers are still on the walls of the deepest cave, older than any wave of the tally, and every wave carved since is carved below them. From the hand-marks come the island's customs: a tally-keeper is made by laying a hand on the cave wall beside the first hands and blowing ochre over it; the caves are entered only at evening, so the elders live at Bukonyo above them and walk down every night; and the names of the dead are counted as waves on the walls and called at the Calling of Names. In the Fever Years of 2A 1211 the elders cut the names of the plague dead into the deepest cave, which the islanders say is cold because of how many names it holds. Since 4A 640 the caves have been the school of the Wave-Tally, where the tally-keepers of every island learn the oldest names, and the other islands send their keepers to Kamu Lamo to lay their hands beside the first.

sign.device: A left hand with its fingers spread, left the dark colour of the rock inside a ragged cloud of blown red ochre, on cave black.
sign.origin: The hand is the hand-mark of the first comers, blown in ochre on the wall of the deepest tally-cave before the first wave of the tally was carved. Every tally-keeper of the south adds a hand beside the first hands at the school of the Wave-Tally, and since the school opened in 4A 640 the elders of Kamu Lamo have flown the ochre-blown hand at the mouth of the caves, so that keepers coming by sea know where to land.
sign.meaning: We were here first and we remember: to the islands a promise that their oldest names are kept, and to strangers who would read the oldest tally the reminder that it is the elders who decide.

dynasties.name: The Elders of the Tally-Caves
dynasties.notable: The island's elders are the keepers of the tally-caves, chosen by the caves' keepers from among themselves; Elder Tikao nau Bukonyo keeps the caves in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Hands in the Cave
events.summary: The first canoe-folk to reach the arcs come ashore on the deep isle and blow red ochre over their hands on the wall of the deepest cave, before the first wave of any tally is carved.

events.name: The Bird Isle
events.summary: The egg-gatherers of the bird isle Kamu Hawin, once called Dunn, put themselves under the elders of the caves, and the guano of the bird isle begins to feed the terraces of the south.

events.name: The Fever Tally
events.summary: In the Fever Years the elders cut the names of the plague dead into the deepest cave, and the islanders still say the cave is cold because of how many names it holds.

events.name: The Tally-Keepers' School
events.summary: The elders begin to teach the tally-keepers of every island in the caves, and Kamu Lamo becomes the school of the Wave-Tally.

countries.capitalReason: Bukonyo, the little hill, is the village above the tally-caves, because the elders who keep the caves must live where they can walk down to them every evening.
countries.today: Kamu Lamo in 4A 1748 is an island of some 40,000 under the elders of the tally-caves, with the bird isle Kamu Hawin. It keeps the oldest tally of the south, teaches the tally-keepers of every island, and gathers eggs and guano for the terraces.

divergence.what: A stranger asks to read the oldest tally and the elders let him.
divergence.consequence: The oldest names of the south are heard outside the islands, and the elders learn whether any of them is a name the north remembers.

divergence.what: The elders close the tally-caves to every foreigner when the war comes.
divergence.consequence: The south keeps its memory to itself, and its tally-keepers become the only people who can say who of the islands died in other people's wars.

countries.name: Kea

founding.story: The terraced isles of the south-western chain, Kea, Agla and the Rice Islands, have little water and grow rice on every slope that will hold it, and in a dry storm year the terrace families of all three swore to share their water by council rather than by war. The terrace council has ruled them since, and the rice of the Rice Islands feeds every island that has a bad harvest.

roots.story: The terraced isles of the south-western chain have little water and the oldest water law of the south. Their tales say that long before Aen the first terrace families of Kea, Agla and the Rice Islands carried with them from the first canoes a block of hard wood cut with two channels, a divider that splits one stream into two equal streams, and set it at the head of the first terrace so that the water would fall equally to every field below. Every terrace of the chain has had a divider since, and the families hold that a field that takes more than its share from the divider steals from the dead who cut the terraces. In the Year of the Dry Wind, 1A 960, the terrace families of all three isles swore to share their water by council rather than by war and dug the cisterns of Tuwang, and the council chooses a Water-Keeper each dry season to hold the great divider of the cisterns. From the divider come the council's customs and its fame. After the Fever Years left the Great Isle's terraces untended, the council sent its rice to every island, and since 2A 1213 no island of the south lets another go hungry. When Agla accused Kea of taking more than its share of the cisterns in 4A 1480, the council sent the quarrel to the elders of the tally-caves, who ruled for Agla, and Kea paid in rice, as the divider's law demands.

sign.device: A forked water-channel splitting one stream into two equal streams, in water silver on terrace brown.
sign.origin: The forked channel is the divider of the first terrace, the block that splits one stream into two equal streams. The great divider of the Tuwang cisterns, held by the Water-Keeper, was cut to its pattern when the Water Oath was sworn in 1A 960, and the council's banner, raised over the cisterns in every dry season, shows the water dividing.
sign.meaning: Equal water for every field: to the terrace families the promise of a fair share, and to any island that takes more than its share the reminder that Kea itself once paid.

dynasties.name: The Terrace Council
dynasties.notable: The heads of the terrace families of Kea, Agla and the Rice Islands sit as one council and choose a Water-Keeper each dry season; Water-Keeper Luanga nau Kea holds the office in 4A 1748.

events.name: The Water Oath
events.summary: In the Year of the Dry Wind the terrace families of Kea, Agla and the Rice Islands swear to share their water by council, and the cisterns of Tuwang are dug.

events.name: The Rice Ships
events.summary: After the Fever Years leave the Great Isle's terraces untended, the terrace council sends its rice to every island, and the guest-right of the south gains the custom that no island lets another go hungry.

events.name: The Cistern Quarrel
events.summary: Agla accuses Kea of taking more than its share of the cisterns in a dry year; the council sends the quarrel to the elders of the tally-caves, who rule for Agla, and Kea pays in rice.

countries.capitalReason: Tuwang, the field town, stands among the largest terraces of Kea, round the cisterns the council dug, because the town that holds the water must be where the council can watch it.
countries.today: Kea in 4A 1748 is a terrace council of some 120,000 rice-growers on Kea, Agla and the Rice Islands under Water-Keeper Luanga. It grows the rice of the south, shares its water by council, and sends rice to any island in a bad year.

divergence.what: In a storm year the terrace council sells its rice to a foreign fleet instead of the islands.
divergence.consequence: The guest-right's promise that no island goes hungry breaks, and the islands learn whose rice they can count on.

divergence.what: A dry storm year empties the cisterns and the council cannot share what it does not have.
divergence.consequence: The islands go hungry together, and the guest-right is tested by hunger instead of by strangers.

countries.name: Sidea

founding.story: The islets at the western arc's end, Sidea, Pon and Yumbo, were too small for a moot each, and in a storm year that cut them off from the Great Isle for a whole season their families chose one elder to speak for all of them. Sidea has had one elder over its islets since, and its drummers of Yumbo beat the elder's summons from islet to islet across the water.

roots.story: The islets at the end of the western arc are the first land of the south that the storms reach and the last that help reaches. Long before Aen, the drummers of Yumbo say, the families of the islets learned to hollow a log into a slit-drum whose voice carries further over water than a man can shout, and used it to call each other across the channels when the storms closed the sea. In the Year of the Long Wind, 2A 300, a storm cut the islets off from the Great Isle for a whole season, and the families chose one elder to speak for all of them; the drummers of Yumbo beat his first summons from islet to islet, and every elder of Sidea since has held office only as long as the drummers will beat his summons. In 3A 700 the drummers learned to beat messages faster than a canoe can sail, and the drum road was born: a storm seen first from the western islets is beaten from drum to drum to the Great Isle before it arrives. From the drums come Sidea's customs: the drummers' consent is the elder's authority; every islet keeps a drum that is never beaten except for the islands; and since the storm year of 4A 1550, when the islets' canoes sank in one night and the three realms of the Great Isle rebuilt them under the guest-right, Sidea has sent its first catch of every year to the drowned shrine. It is the first land of the islands that a ship blown south from the West sees.

sign.device: An upright slit-drum hollowed from a log, its long slit facing outward, in drum-wood brown on storm grey.
sign.origin: The slit-drum is the drum of Yumbo that beat the first elder's summons in 2A 300 and the first warning of the drum road in 3A 700. It stands under its own roof at Yumbo and is carried to the harbour of Ponwan when the elder calls the islets together, and the islets' banner has shown it since the drummers made the first elder.
sign.meaning: The first warning: to the Great Isle a promise that the islets will always beat the storm's coming, and to the elder the reminder that the drums choose whom they summon for.

dynasties.name: The Elders of the Western Islets
dynasties.notable: One elder is chosen by the families of all the islets and holds the office until the drummers of Yumbo will no longer beat his summons; Elder Nuoan nau Pon holds it in 4A 1748.

events.name: One Elder
events.summary: In the Year of the Long Wind the islets, cut off for a season, choose one elder to speak for them all, and the drummers of Yumbo beat his first summons.

events.name: The Drum Road
events.summary: The drummers of Yumbo learn to beat messages from islet to islet faster than a canoe can sail, and the western arc warns the Great Isle of every storm it sees first.

events.name: The Lost Canoes
events.summary: A storm year sinks the islets' fishing canoes in a single night, and the Great Isle's three realms rebuild them under the guest-right; Sidea still sends its first catch of every year to the drowned shrine.

countries.capitalReason: Ponwan, the harbour of Pon, is the one sheltered anchorage at the end of the western arc, where the canoes of all the islets can lie together in a storm and the elder can be found by anyone who sails in.
countries.today: Sidea in 4A 1748 is a cluster of islets of some 60,000 under one elder, Nuoan, at the end of the western arc with Pon and Yumbo. Its drummers carry the first warning of every storm to the Great Isle, and it is the first land of the islands that a ship blown south from the West sees.

divergence.what: A ship blown far south from the West makes its first landfall at the western islets.
divergence.consequence: The elder decides whether to send the wreck on to the Great Isle's house for the shipwrecked or keep its survivors on Pon, and the drums carry the news before the ship is beached.

divergence.what: In the war the drummers of Yumbo refuse to beat any foreign fleet's summons.
divergence.consequence: The islands lose their warning road while the fleets are at sea, and the western arc keeps to itself.

cities.name: Suyowan
cities.legend: On the founding day of every storm year the Priest-Elders row out over the drowned shrine and read the tally into the water, and the islanders say the names come back on the next tide, which is why the lagoon is never quiet.
cities.economy: The shrine's pilgrims on the Reef Road, lagoon fish-traps, salt from Angsun, the safest anchorage of the islands.

cities.name: Shrine Beneath the Tide
cities.legend: Over the drowned door a name is carved that the islanders read as Aen; the tally-keepers repeat it at every Calling of Names, and they say it is needed, though no one on the island can say what for.
cities.economy: None but the offerings of names brought by the Reef Road.

cities.name: Lamowan
cities.legend: In the house for the shipwrecked every stranger is given a mat, a bowl and a month alone, and the people of Lamowan say the sea sends them one good guest for every ten bad ones, which is a better rate than the land manages.
cities.economy: Rice terraces of the Tich, pearl-diving, whaling on the Yowi-yoor coast, the house for the shipwrecked.

cities.name: Pelo Tamo
cities.legend: The clan hall of Pelo Tamo has a mast for a ridge-pole, and the timber-folk say the hall will stand until the last Verdean ship comes home, so they never let the last one leave.
cities.economy: Hull-timber for Aenor Isle, canoe-building, pilots hired to any ship.

cities.name: Riwang
cities.legend: The elders of Riwang count the boats out at dawn and in at dusk, and the fishers say that a boat counted in after dark is not one of theirs, whatever it looks like.
cities.economy: Day fishing on the reef, dried fish, shell.

cities.name: Yongwa
cities.legend: The ring-council meets round a fire of driftwood that every Yong village must bring a stick for, and the islanders say the year a village brings none, the lagoon will burn again.
cities.economy: Lagoon fish-traps, shell-carving of Jingar, rope and nets of Torsor, shrine stone of Yongrost.

cities.name: Bukonyo
cities.legend: Above the tally-caves the elders say the deepest cave is cold because of how many names it holds, and the tally-keepers who come to learn are made to sleep one night in it before they are taught.
cities.economy: The school of the tally-keepers, eggs and guano from Kamu Hawin.

cities.name: Tuwang
cities.legend: The cisterns of Tuwang were dug in the Year of the Dry Wind, and the terrace families say a Water-Keeper who lies about the water in them will find his own terrace dry the next season.
cities.economy: Rice of the terraces and the Rice Islands, the council's cisterns.

cities.name: Ponwan
cities.legend: The drummers of Yumbo beat the elder's summons to Ponwan across the water, and the islet-folk say a summons that is not answered by the third drum means the elder must be chosen again.
cities.economy: Fishing, drum-making, the first sight of ships from the West.

cities.name: Lua
cities.legend: On the volcano islet the Priest-Elders built a shrine at the foot of the smoking slope in the Year of Ash, and the islanders say the mountain has stayed quiet only because the tally is read there every dry season.
cities.economy: Ash-soil gardens, sulphur gathered for the salt-pans of Angsun.

figures.name: Nuoyo nau Enhis
figures.role: First Priest-Elder of the Tide Shrine
figures.biography: A tally-keeper of the lagoon villages who swam down to the drowned shrine after the Rising Tide of 2A 40 to read the carved name and came up alive, Nuoyo was made the first Priest-Elder and founded the Calling of Names beneath the water.

figures.name: Maiyan nau Lamowan
figures.role: Builder of the house for the shipwrecked
figures.biography: A terrace-head of Howan who lost her family in the Fever Years and still argued in the moot against turning strangers back into the sea, Maiyan proposed the house at Lamowan where the wrecked are fed and kept apart for a month, and so saved both the guest-right and the islands' health.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The guest-right
lawsAndCustoms.summary: Every stranger the sea throws ashore is fed and housed, and to harm a guest is the worst crime of the south; since the Fever Years Howan keeps the wrecked apart for a month first, and since 2A 1213 no island lets another go hungry.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The storm years
lawsAndCustoms.summary: The islanders name each year after its great storm and count its months by the tides; the twelve months of the north are used only with foreign captains.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The Wave-Tally
lawsAndCustoms.summary: The dead of each island are counted as waves on the reef and on the walls of the tally-caves, and the names are called at the Calling of Names; the islanders say the names are needed.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The Reef Road
lawsAndCustoms.summary: Every islander may walk the Reef Road to the drowned shrine to bring a name for the tally, and the three realms of the Great Isle keep the peace on the road and in the year of every pilgrimage.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The Day Rule
lawsAndCustoms.summary: The reef off Ancha is fished only by day, and nobody of Nara crosses the Night Reef after dark.
